title: try, catch, finally, and filters (handling specific failures)
hook: try marks risky work. catch handles a failure type you understand. finally always runs for that try — even when you rethrow. A when filter lets you catch a subset without swallowing everything else.

sections.heading: What are try, catch, and finally?

blocks.text: A **try** block wraps code that might throw. One or more **catch** blocks handle specific exception types — the runtime picks the first compatible handler. A **finally** block always runs for that try, whether the try succeeded, was caught, or rethrew. More-derived exception types must appear before less-derived ones, or the compiler errors because the later catch would be unreachable. The **when** keyword adds a filter so you can catch only exceptions that match an extra condition.

entries.plainDefinition: A block of code where exceptions may occur. Control leaves immediately when throw runs.
A handler for a specific exception type. Only runs if the thrown type is compatible.
Cleanup code that always executes for its try — success, catch, or rethrow. The basis for using statements.
An optional condition on a catch clause. The catch runs only if the type matches AND the filter returns true.

blocks.text: Correct try/catch structure keeps workers honest. An Amazon Simple Queue Service (SQS) consumer should retry throttling (HTTP 429) but let programming bugs bubble. finally guarantees leases, locks, and temporary state release even when an exception flies through. Without when filters, you either catch too much or duplicate catch blocks.

blocks.title: finally runs before return
blocks.body: A return inside try still executes finally before the method actually returns. Do not put logic in finally that throws — a finally throw can hide the original exception.

items.title: try runs normally
items.body: If no throw occurs, catch blocks are skipped and finally runs.

items.title: throw triggers catch search
items.body: The runtime finds the first catch whose type matches. If a when filter is present, it must also evaluate to true.

items.title: catch handles or rethrows
items.body: The catch body runs. throw; (without an identifier) rethrows and preserves the stack trace.

items.title: finally always runs
items.body: Whether the try succeeded, a catch handled the error, or a rethrow is in flight, finally executes before leaving the try scope.

diagram.title: try / catch / finally flow
diagram.source:
flowchart TD
  START[Enter try] --> RUN[Execute try body]
  RUN -->|success| FIN[Run finally]
  RUN -->|throw| MATCH{Matching catch?}
  MATCH -->|yes + when ok| CATCH[Run catch body]
  MATCH -->|no| FIN2[Run finally on unwind path]
  CATCH --> FIN
  FIN --> DONE[Continue or return]
  FIN2 --> BUBBLE[Exception continues up stack]

snippet.explanation: Line 5: cancellation with the token is expected — rethrow with throw;. Line 8: 429 Too Many Requests gets a retry. Line 12: other HTTP failures log and rethrow. Line 17: lease release always runs.

snippet.label: Most-derived catch must come first
snippet.explanation: Line 6: ArgumentNullException is more derived than ArgumentException, so it must appear first. Reversing the order is a compile error because the broader catch would swallow the specific one.

snippet.explanation: Line 8: finally deletes the temp file whether upload succeeded or threw. This is the manual pattern that using automates for IDisposable types.

blocks.title: try/catch in C# vs JS/TS
rows: catch (e) — any thrown value; TS types e as unknown
No built-in equivalent — inspect inside catch
Single catch — type checks are manual if/else

blocks.title: Empty catch blocks
blocks.body: catch (Exception) { } hides bugs and loses data in workers. If you catch, log, restore state, or rethrow. Never succeed a queue message after swallowing an unknown failure.

blocks.title: Side effects inside when filters
blocks.body: when should be fast and side-effect free. Logging or mutating state inside a filter makes debugging nightmares. Throwing inside a filter is especially nasty.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: exceptions are for exceptional control flow — they are expensive (stack walk, allocation) and poison hot paths. Many teams adopt Result<T> or OneOf-style returns for expected failures (validation, not-found) and reserve exceptions for truly unexpected faults. In an SQS worker, catch transient HttpRequestException with when filters for retry, but return Result.Failure for business rule violations instead of throw — the message completes without stack churn. Rust and Go bias Result; C# BCL still throws — know when to wrap at your boundary. finally still runs on success paths — prefer using for IDisposable over manual finally when possible.

snippet.label: Exception versus Result at a service boundary
snippet.explanation: Lines 1–8: expected CSV problems return Result — no exception cost. Lines 11–14: throw only when the caller asserted success — bug or catastrophic path.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Expected validation on every row in CSV import
Replacing every BCL throw without wrapping
Logging or DB calls inside filter
Logic that throws and hides original

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Empty catch (Exception) { }. Using exceptions for normal control flow on every request. Not knowing finally runs before return. Saying Result replaces all exceptions with no tradeoff discussion.

interviewTakeaways: Most-derived catch first; finally always runs for that try.
when filters select subsets — keep them side-effect free.
Result/Try* for expected failures; exceptions for exceptional paths.
60s: catch at worker boundary with when for transient faults. Result for expected failures. throw; preserves stack. Empty catch rejected.
Follow-up: how does exception cost compare to returning Result on a hot CSV path?
commonPitfalls: Empty catch blocks get you rejected immediately.
Exceptions for every validation row without measuring cost.
Strong answer: 'Result for expected outcomes. Exceptions for exceptional. when for transient catch. finally always runs. throw; not throw ex.'

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript has the same three keywords but no typed catch (except optional catch binding). There is no when filter — you inspect properties inside the catch body.
TypeScript cannot catch only TypeError at the type level — anything might be thrown. C# can catch only IOException and let others bubble.
